title: Burst fragmentation session sampler runbook
content:
Purpose:
This is a short lab-style runbook documenting a focused microbenchmark comparing how session fragmentation (many short sessions interleaved vs fewer long sessions) affects tail latency and amortized cost under two slotization strategies: slot-tiling and opportunistic-prefetch. The aim is to create a compact, copy-pasteable narrative plus ASCII charts so product/console folks can turn this into a one-pager.

Scope and hypotheses:
- Workloads: synthetic chat sessions representative of embedding+chat mix (70% chat turns, 30% lightweight embedding calls).
- Shapes tested: 
  * Sparse-microburst: 10k sessions over 10 minutes, median length 3 turns, high interarrival jitter (bursty).
  * Steady-long: 2k sessions over 10 minutes, median length 25 turns, smooth arrival.
- Hypothesis: fragmentation (many short sessions) increases p99 latency under tile allocation because tiling amortization is lower; opportunistic-prefetch reduces p99 but increases mean-cost due to redundant warms.

Test harness (quick notes):
- Runtime: internal dev cluster (g4-like equivalent nodes), same model weights v2 (fp16), batcher=continuous with window=20ms.
- Load generator: modified wrk-like shim sampling session lengths from empirical distribution (attached as CSV in linked artifacts).
- Metrics collected: p50/p90/p99 latency (ms) end-to-end, tokens per second, tail-kv-hit ratio, per-request cost estimate ($ per 1k tokens using internal price sheet).
- Run length: 15 minute warmup + 10 minute collection window. 3 runs per scenario.

Config knobs (what we toggled):
- Allocation strategy: slot-tiling vs opportunistic-prefetch
- KV cache TTL: 30s vs 300s
- Session affinity: enabled vs disabled
- Quantization profile: baseline (fp16)

Raw observations (representative single-run averaged values):
ASCII summary table (fragmentation vs steady):

Scenario            | p50(ms) | p90(ms) | p99(ms) | tokens/sec | $/1k tokens
--------------------|---------|---------|---------|------------|-----------
Sparse-microburst   | 48      | 154     | 410     | 5.8k       | 0.62
Sparse-microburst*  | 60      | 120     | 220     | 6.3k       | 0.78
Steady-long         | 30      | 65      | 120     | 9.6k       | 0.45
Steady-long*        | 35      | 75      | 140     | 9.1k       | 0.52

Legend: rows with * = opportunistic-prefetch enabled (TTL=300s), others = slot-tiling default (TTL=30s). Numbers are illustrative from lab runs.

Interpretation notes:
- Tail latency (p99) for the sparse-microburst under slot-tiling is high (410ms). Tile-tiling suffers because many short sessions prevent steady batching; allocator keeps many small slots partially filled leading to more warmup overhead per turn.
- Opportunistic-prefetch reduces p99 significantly for the microburst case (down to 220ms) at the cost of higher per-token spend (0.78 vs 0.62 $/1k). The prefetch policy warms more KV/prefix state and so has higher tokens/sec (slightly) but wastes compute on sessions that do not continue.
- For steady-long workload, the difference between strategies is smaller: tiling already amortizes well (p99 120ms). Prefetch adds modest cost and slightly increases throughput variance.

ASCII microchart: p99 vs scenario & strategy (ms)
Sparse-microburst: 410ms [##########] (tiling)
Sparse-microburst*: 220ms [#####     ] (prefetch)
Steady-long:        120ms [##        ] (tiling)
Steady-long*:       140ms [###       ] (prefetch)

Decision heuristics (short):
- If >60% sessions <6 turns and burstiness index >0.6 -> recommend opportunistic-prefetch with TTL 120-300s for p99-sensitive tiers.
- If workload median length >15 turns -> prefer slot-tiling to minimize $/k tokens and keep steady latency.
- For mixed tenants: set per-tenant policy with canary window for 24–72h; default to slot-tiling for free tier and prefetch for enterprise p99 SLA tiers.

Checklist to operationalize in Console (todo):
- [ ] Add UI toggle: "Burst fragmentation mitigation" with quick presets (Tile-mode, Prefetch-fast, Prefetch-conservative).
- [ ] Wire per-tenant telemetry: show fraction of sessions <6 turns, burstiness index, p99 delta if switched.
- [ ] Add recommended cost estimate card that shows delta $/1k tokens when enabling prefetch.

Open questions / unknowns:
- Where is the inflection point for TTL (30s vs 120s vs 300s) across different hardware families? We only tested g4-like nodes here.
- How does quantized int8 affect warmup penalty and p99 for microbursts? Hypothesis: quantization may amplify cold-start jitter; needs microbench.
- Multi-tenant interference: does prefetch warmup increase noisy neighbor p99 on heterogenous racks? (observed small CPU bump in this lab).

Appendix: quick-run reproduction notes (commands):
- generator: python tools/session_gen.py --shape sparse-microburst --qps 350 --duration 15m --out microburst.csv
- runner: bin/loadrun --policy slot-tiling --kv-ttl 30 --model v2 --load microburst.csv --collect 10m --metrics out/microburst-tiling.json
- convert: tools/plot_ascii.py out/microburst-tiling.json > out/microburst-tiling-ascii.txt

References and links:
- Confluence notes: CONFLUENCE-1234 (fragmentation concepts)
- GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/tiling-bench/pull/42 (load generator and harness)
- Jira: JIRA-INFRA-987 (follow-up: run int8 microbench)

Short next steps (for product & console):
1) Validate TTL sweep 30/60/120/300s on A100 cluster (2 runs, 3 seeds).
2) Add delta card prototype in console with toggles and estimated p99 impact using this runbook's heuristics.
3) Schedule cross-team review with platform-eng and serving-runtime to evaluate noisy-neighbor risks.

Notes-to-self (informal):
- Keep the microbench small-ish so eng can reproduce in ~1h.
- Capture a run with packet-capture next time to confirm whether network tails correlate with p99 spikes (saw minor correlation).

End of runbook.

(If you want a trimmed one-pager extract for sales collateral, ping me and I will flatten the decision heuristics and the ASCII microchart into a 1-column doc.)
